They take your f5 pawn, but they are ignoring the storm on the queenside. Take on b6 to open lines to their king.
Your knight grabs a7, but Rxa7 was much stronger and faster. Lesson: in the attack, use your rooks on open files — they hit hardest.
Their king runs to b7 into the open. Now Nb5 sets up a deadly net around the king.
You push c4 to attack, but it lets the king breathe — Qa4 kept the king trapped tight. Lesson: in a mating attack, keep checking and cut off escape squares.
They block with Be7, but their king is still in great danger. Rook to e1 adds more pieces to the attack.
Huge blunder — the king steps to b7 and walks into a forced mate. Play Qa7+ and it is checkmate in two.
This is the start of trouble: Nf6 walks into e5. Better was Bb6, keeping the bishop safe and ready. Lesson: before moving, ask 'can a pawn attack this piece?'
They push e5 and now your f6 knight is attacked and must run. This was their strong plan from the c3 move — your center is falling apart.
Ng4 saves the knight but puts it on the edge doing little; Nh7 was the safer retreat. Your king side is getting thin.
Bb4 pins nothing useful and ignores your king; d5 was better to hit their center and free your game. Lesson: when behind, fix king safety first.
Nb4 is a blunder that allows mate; O-O (castling) was needed to hide the king. Sadly nothing was protecting f7 now. Lesson: always check 'is my king about to be mated?' before anything else.
Black made a mistake here. Take the pawn with dxe5 and you win a free pawn — it is not protected.
Black weakened his king with g6. You can jump in with Qf6, putting your queen on a strong, annoying square.
Castling is safe, but pushing e4 was much stronger — it grabs the center and opens lines for your pieces. Lesson: when you are better, look to attack before defending.
Black blundered. Play cxd5 — after the trades you win a piece because his pieces get overloaded on d5.
You develop the other knight. Pushing the pawn to e5 would have grabbed more space, but this is fine.
Black tucks the king safe by castling. You can still grab space with the e5 push when ready.
You place the bishop on an active line toward Black's king. The e5 pawn push was even stronger.
You develop the bishop. Slightly better was Ne2 to reroute the knight; the bishop here can be poked later. Lesson: develop where the enemy can't easily kick you.
Black pushes a pawn that doesn't really threaten you. You stay comfortable with more space.

Mistake — this bishop move drops your e5 pawn. Black could play Nxe5! and if you take with the knight, the queen grabs your bishop. Better was Rfe1 to guard e5. Lesson: count the defenders of a pawn before moving away.
Lucky for you — Black missed Nxe5 and played the queen out instead. Your e5 pawn survives; now defend it again.
Black's queen slides to eye your b2 pawn. Watch that pawn now.
You grab space on the side. Keeping the rooks active with Rfe1 was a touch better. Lesson: rooks belong on open or soon-to-open files.
You leap the knight to a bold outpost. Be3 first was cleaner; the e5 pawn still needs care. Lesson: finish guarding before the flashy jump.
Black grabs your b2 pawn with the queen — but it's deep in your camp. Trap it: Rab1 hits the queen.
You attack the queen with a rook, good idea — but Rab1 (the corner rook) was the right one. Lesson: use the rook that keeps the most pressure.
Big blunder — Black moves the knight and leaves the queen hanging. Punish now: Rxb2 simply wins the queen.
You contest the file, but pushing the a-pawn was clearly stronger here. Lesson: when ahead, race your passed pawn to promote.
You swing the knight toward Black's king side. Trading with Bf6 was stronger, but you keep pressure on f7. Lesson: aim pieces at weak squares near the king.
Black grabs your e5 pawn but leaves f7 weak. Punish: Ndxf7! forks into Black's position.
Black's bishop wanders and misses defending. The crushing path was Nh6+ then Nxe6+ winning more.
You grab the e6 pawn, still winning — but Nh6+ first was even stronger. Lesson: a check often comes before the capture.
Game-ending blunder — this pawn push lets you mate. Punish at once: Nh6+ forces the king to f8, then Nxh7 is checkmate.
White plays e3, a weak move. Jump your knight to b4 here — it hits weak squares and gives you a clear edge.
White plays Nc3, again missing the better d4. Now Nb4 is strong — go for it!
White plays Qe2, a big blunder. Take with Ngxf2! It wins material and wrecks White's position.
You play Ndxf2, but with the wrong knight — Ngxf2 was the way. Still, you win material here. Lesson: when two pieces can capture, check which order wins more.
You play Bf5 and miss it badly — Nxh1 wins the rook! This was a big chance lost. Lesson: when a rook is sitting in the corner, grab it before saving smaller things.
You play Bc5, but castling with O-O-O was much safer and better. Lesson: when you can castle to safety, usually do it.
White plays Rg1, a blunder. Castle long with O-O-O now — your king gets safe and you stay on top.
You play b5, which weakens the squares near your own king — Qd7 was much safer. Lesson: be careful pushing pawns in front of your own king.
You play Kc7, but it leaves f7 weak — h5 was better. Now White can hit f7.
White plays Nxc6, a big blunder! Take with Rxc6 and you win a whole knight.
You play Kd6, sending the king the wrong way — Kb6 was better and safer. Lesson: in the endgame, walk your king toward your own pawns, not into the enemy knights.
White plays Ke3, a blunder. Swing your rook to a2 and win White's loose pawns.
You push g4, but Ra2 was much stronger to grab pawns.
White plays Nf4. The engine wanted Ned4; you can play Rg3 to hold your pawn.
You play Rg3, but Ra2 was again the better, more active rook move.
White plays Be4, a blunder. Take the knight with gxf3 — you win a piece.
You play Ke5, walking into trouble — Rg1 was much safer. Now White can check and fork. Lesson: keep your king away from squares where a knight can check it.
White plays Nd3+, check, which gains time on your king. Step the king back to d6.
White plays Ke2. Bring your rook to the most active square you can find.
White plays Ba6, a blunder, putting the bishop where you can take it. Play Rxa6 and win the bishop!

This drops material: now White can play Ne3, hitting your queen on d5 AND your bishop on f5 at once. Bc7 kept the bishop safe instead. Lesson: your queen sat on d5 a long time — loose pieces get forked.
White trades his strong knight for your bishop — a gift that lets you off the hook. Just take back.
Too greedy — this grabs a side pawn but your queen gets trapped in the corner after Rb1. Qxe4 took a safe central pawn instead. Lesson: don't chase pawns into the corner with your queen.
A big slip by White — this push loosens his pieces. Play Bf8 to tuck the bishop safe, then win the a4 pawn with Qxa4.
This lets White hit your bishop with Nd3 and later wreck your kingside with Bxf6. Bf8 first kept everything solid. Lesson: tuck loose pieces to safety before grabbing pawns.

This hangs the bishop: White plays Rxe7, and after you take back, e5 forks and wins your knight. Qxa4 was the move — grab a pawn and trade queens. Lesson: check what your move leaves open before playing it.
Taking back opens your own king, and the f6 pawn falls to Bxf6 anyway. The active Qd2 made more trouble. Lesson: when behind, look for counterplay instead of sad recaptures.
A mistake by White, leaving the bishop loose in the middle. Hit it with Nd7 to gain time.
White's queen drops back. Now f6 attacks the e5 bishop and can win it.
You miss it again — f6 (or Nxe5) wins the strong bishop; instead the king walks to the corner. Keep the king near the center with Ke7. Lesson: when a piece is hanging, take it.
White gives up the bishop with check — good for you. Take it back.
Wrong way — the king heads to the corner. In endgames the king should march to the center, so Ke7 was better. Lesson: in the endgame your king is a fighter — bring it forward.
Black grabs your e4 pawn with the knight, but this is a big blunder. Just take it back with Nxe4 — you win a whole knight.
You retreat to b3, but this lets Black push c4 and trap the knight idea. The check Bb5+ first was much better and kept Black tangled up.
Black brings the bishop to f5. He is just developing; you can play d3 to challenge his strong e4 pawn.
Black pushes d4 instead of trading. Now you can simply grab the pawn with dxe4, staying well ahead.
Black pushes e3 to poke your position. Just take it with fxe3 and your pawns are fine.
Black plays Nd4 to jump into the middle. You can trade it off with Nxd4 and stay comfortable.
You give a check with Nc7+, planning to grab the rook. It wins the rook but loses time; the calm Qf3 kept a cleaner game.
Black plays Bd6 to attack your bishop. You can trade it off safely with Bxd6 and keep your extra material.
You play Qf3, but this is a serious slip. Bxd6 first removed the dangerous bishop; now Black gets a strong attack on your king.
Black takes your bishop with check (Bxg3+). Take back the right way with Qxg3, not the pawn, to keep your king safer.
You recapture with the pawn (hxg3). This opens lines near your king; Qxg3 was the safer way to take.
Black plays g6, a slow move that helps you. Get your bishop out with Be2 and rush to castle your king to safety.
You check with Qd5+. A trade with Qc7+ was stronger; it would swap queens and kill Black's attack.
Black blocks with the bishop on d7. You can give a strong check with Qa5+ and trade queens to be safe.
Big gift — instead of grabbing g7, White's bishop drifted to g4. Just castle short with O-O and you stand well.
You castle long, but your king is safer on the other side; O-O was the move. Lesson: castle toward the safer, better-guarded side.
Big slip by White — this push loses the thread. Punish it with Nf6, putting your knight to work and hitting back in the center.
The knight leaps to e5 but Qh5 just chases it and you lose time. Nf6 was stronger. Lesson: a fancy square is no good if the queen kicks the piece at once.
White misses the chase and plays quietly; you're okay, so reroute your knight to a good post.
The knight steps back to guard but turns passive and lets White grow. Qb5 offered a queen trade and eased your troubles. Lesson: trading queens is a great way to calm a hard position.
Bringing the rook over walks into trouble on the pinned knight. Nd5 jumped the knight to a strong, safe square. Lesson: with a pinned piece, free it — don't pile more onto the pin.
White grabs the knight, but this trade actually helps you. Take back with your e8-rook (Rexe7) and you're right back in the game.
Blocking with the rook is too passive and ties your pieces down. Just move the king with Kc8. Lesson: don't use a strong rook as a shield when the king can simply step aside.
White's rook swings to the b-file to attack; give your king some air and guard the queenside.
The king steps out, but a6 first made a safe pocket and slowed White down. Lesson: before moving the king, give it a safe square to run to.
White plays a slow move instead of pressing; use the breather to activate your rook and queen.
White blocks its own pawn with the bishop — a passive, weak move. You can hit the center with d5 to use this chance.
Bc5 develops a piece, but d5 was clearly better — it attacks the center and opens lines for your pieces. Lesson: when the center is loose, push a pawn there instead of just developing.
Be6 is a mistake — your knight still sits at home. Nc6 was clearly better to develop and control the center. Lesson: get your knights out before fancy bishop moves.
Big blunder by White! Pushing f4 leaves the e4 pawn loose — you can win it with Nxe4 right now.
Bd7 saves the bishop but you missed Nxe4 a second time — that pawn was still free. Lesson: when a piece can be taken for nothing, grab it.
b6 is a mistake — c4 was much better to keep your strong bishop firing at f2. Lesson: keep your active pieces working, don't block their lines.
White blunders by taking on b6. Take back with Qxb6 — your queen comes out with power.
A fatal blunder! White's bishop leaves f2 undefended, and your queen and bishop are aiming right at it — Qxf2 is checkmate.
Checkmate! Your queen lands on f2, protected by the a7-bishop you set up long ago. Beautiful finish — well done!
Big mistake by Black — Nxd5 helps you. Just recapture with exd5! Your pawn takes space and opens the e-file for your rook.
Careful! b3 dropped your c2 pawn. c3 was safe. After this Black grabs c2 with the rook. Lesson: before a quiet pawn move, check what it leaves undefended.
Black pushes b4 and attacks your queen, another inaccuracy by him. Play Qa4+ to check and untangle while staying way ahead.
Slip — Re1 wastes time and lets Black get active. Rxc2 was strong, trading and grabbing the b-pawn. Lesson: when ahead, trade pieces and don't drift.
Black pushes a5 to support his b-pawn. You can play a3 to challenge it. Keep things controlled.
Black plays Bd7. Now axb4 opens lines and you can pick off his weak pawns. Keep pushing your edge.
Black pushes b3 but this drops the bishop! Take it: Rxa4 wins the piece. His passed pawn won't be enough. Grab it!
Black gives a desperate check with Rh1+. Just take it: Kxh1 — it's a free rook and ends his tricks. Take it!
Your opponent put their bishop on e5, right in the middle, but this loses time. You can simply take it with your knight (Nxe5) and come out ahead.
Big mistake by your opponent — the knight jump to g4 leaves them much worse. Punish it with e5! This pawn push attacks the f6 knight and gains a strong center.

You took with the bishop (Bxf6), which throws away most of your edge. exf6 was much stronger — it wins the knight and keeps a big lead. Lesson: when two captures are possible, check which one wins more.
Rook to f3 looks aggressive but it drops a lot of your advantage. dxc4 was better — it wins a pawn and keeps you safe. Lesson: finish grabbing free material before getting fancy.
Your opponent pushes e5, which is a slip. The strong reply is Qh5, keeping your queen active and eyeing their king.
Your opponent plays b6 and misses their best defense. Jump in with Ne4! Your knight heads for f6 with check and joins the attack.

Rh3 is a serious blunder — it hangs the rook and your opponent can just take it with the bishop. Ne4 was the move, sending the knight in with a strong attack. Lesson: before moving, check if the square is guarded by an enemy piece.
Your opponent grabs your f4 pawn with the queen. Bring your knight to d5 — it is active and helps your attack.
Ne4 is okay but Nd5 was stronger, hitting more squares near their king. Keep fighting — your attack is still alive.
Your opponent moves the rook to g8. You can calmly tuck your king with Kg1 to stay safe before continuing.
You take the pawn, but d4 was much stronger. Lesson: when the enemy king is open, hit the center to open lines instead of grabbing a side pawn.
This grabs a pawn but lets Black hit back hard — d4 was much better. Lesson: keep your strong center instead of chasing one pawn.
They blunder! This drops material. Play Ng3, which attacks the bishop on f5 and wins time.
You trade with check. Ng3 was a bit better, but this is okay and simplifies the game.
A check that loses time; Nd4 was better for them. Just block with c3, which also kicks the bishop.
A big miss. Bxc6 was the move — it wins material by taking the knight. Lesson: before a fancy plan, check for a simple capture first.
You take the bishop, but Be3 was better. Still, taking a piece is fine.
Huge blunder! Now you win the queen. Play Be6+ — after they block, you take the queen. This is a winning fork on the king and queen.
A knight check that forks; Rhf8 was better for them. The safe king move Kh1 keeps everything fine.
This drops material to Bxf2+. Kh1 was safe. Lesson: when checked, move the king to a safe square before giving up a piece.
King goes the wrong way and loses the bishop. Kg1 was safe. Lesson: in a check, pick the square that keeps your pieces protected.
Kf1 was better. The king is getting pushed around.
Kc2 was safer. Lesson: when picking a king move, avoid squares that allow a fork.
A passive rook move; their rooks were stronger staying active. Use this break to push your pawns or check.

Careful — Bxf7+ looks scary but it does not work and gives away your good bishop. The simple Nxd4 just won you a piece, because Black's knight was not protected. Lesson: count the pieces before you sacrifice; only give up material if you truly win it back.
Small slip: Qf3+ lets the win slip. You could have played Qxe5 to simply win a free pawn. Lesson: before checking, ask if a quiet capture wins more.
Black blunders with Qc6. Now Qd5 hits hard, lining up to win the e5 pawn and tangle Black up.
Black plays a6 to push your knight, which wastes a move. You can calmly retreat with N5c3 and stay better.

Big mistake — Bf6 leaves your bishop where Black's queen just takes it for free. Bxe7 first would have traded safely. Lesson: before moving a piece next to the enemy queen, check if it can simply be captured.
Black plays Nc6, which slips. The strong reply was Nd5, jumping into the hole and hitting the black queen.
Nf3 develops, but again Nd5 was the powerful square for your knight. Lesson: a knight on a central hole the enemy can't chase is golden.
Black pushes g4, which only opens lines toward their own king. Just take it with hxg4.
Black blunders badly with Bxg4. Now Qxb7 grabs a pawn and attacks, and your threats roll in.
Black takes on f3, but it loses — Qxc6+ wins the knight with check. Snap it up.
Black plays Re8, a slip. You have a faster way in, but you can also just keep grabbing pawns.
Qxc7+ wins another pawn with check — very tempting and still winning. The fancy Rdg1 was even sharper, but this is great. Lesson: when ahead, simple and safe wins games.
Black blunders with Qf8, leaving the king wide open. The crushing path was Qd7, pinning and tying Black down completely.
Rh5 is still strong and keeps you totally winning, but Qd7 would have finished things faster. Lesson: when several moves win, pick the one that goes straight for the king.
Black blocks with Bf6, but it collapses. Rf5 sets up a forced mate in a couple of moves.
Small slip by your opponent — they should have grabbed your pawn with exd5. You are free to take their e4 pawn next with dxe4.
Big mistake. Your bishop went to c5 where their knight grabs it for free with Nxc5, and you lose a whole piece. Lesson: before moving, check if the square is attacked — Nc6 was safe.
They place a rook on e1, a slightly loose move. Your plan b5 (which you play next) is the right idea.
They play c3, a weak move that lets you take over. Push c4 to gain space and trap pieces.
Mistake — Bf5 lets their knight come to e5. Pushing c4 was much stronger, gaining space and bothering their pieces.
They take your knight with Bxf6, but this helps you — just recapture with gxf6.
They grab the c4 pawn with the bishop — a blunder. Take the bishop back with bxc4 and you win material.
Mistake — Re2 lets them take on c4. Bringing the bishop to e2 to win their knight was much stronger.
Their knight to d4 is a slip. Grab the a2 pawn with Rxa2 and keep your rooks active.
Mistake — Ba6 lets their knight come to f5 with annoying ideas. Be4 kept your bishop powerful in the middle.
Their Nf3 is a slip. Smash through with Rxf2 — you grab a pawn and keep attacking.
Mistake — Bb7 lets their c-pawn push forward. Playing h5 first to trap the knight was better.
Huge blunder — they play Nf5 and miss your crusher. Start with Rxg2+! and you win on the spot with checks.
You missed the win — h5 lets them off the hook. Rxg2+ and a string of checks was a forced victory.
Their pawn makes a queen with check, but it is loose. Just take it with Bxc8 — the new queen is yours.
Their knight to d5 is a slip. Calmly play Kg7 to stay safe and keep your rook strong.
Your king goes to g6. It works, but g7 was a hair safer from knight checks.
Their rook comes to a1 to bother you. Keep your bishop and rook working together.
You play a6 to guard your pawn. Fine, the position is still good for you.
Their Nb6 is a slip. Save your bishop with Bb7 and stay in control.
Their Nc5 is a slip. Check with Rh1+ to drive the king and win their other rook.
Their king comes to d2 to chase the pawn. Keep your rook guarding the pawn so it can keep going.
Big blunder — Kc2 lets you win their knight. Take it with Rxb7 and the rest is easy.
Black plays c6, a slow move that wastes time (a 1-pawn-level slip). Take the free moment to improve — Qe2 brings your queen into play.
Big gift! Black plays Bxh3?? and just gives up the bishop. Take it: gxh3 wins the piece for free. Lesson: when a piece grabs a pawn next to your king, check if you can simply take it back.
Rc1 lets Black snatch your h3 pawn. Bf1 was better — it guards h3 and shields your king. Lesson: when ahead, keep things safe instead of drifting.
Ng5 looks like it attacks the queen, but it loses material; Bg3 was much safer. Lesson: don't lunge a piece forward if it can just be chased and lost.
Black plays h6 (a real slip — Nxe5 was their strong move). Punish it with Nh3, saving your knight and keeping the game in your favor.
Ne4 drops material; Nh3 was the safe square. Lesson: when your piece is attacked, first find a safe escape before trying something fancy.
Black plays Bxe5 and wins your center pawn. This hurts, but stay focused and look for the best way to fight back.
Bxe5 takes back, but Bg3 was better and kept things together. After this Black just trades and stays ahead. Lesson: count the trade fully before you recapture.
Black plays Nxd3 (a slip — Rad8 was stronger). Punish it simply: cxd3 wins the knight back.
They push b5, gaining space on the side. It looks scary but it weakens their pawns. You still want to play d4 in the middle.
They take back with the g-pawn, but this badly breaks the shield around their king. This is a big blunder. Punish it now with Knight to e4, heading straight for the weak king.
They retreat the queen to d8 — a game-losing blunder; it stops guarding the kingside. Strike with Knight takes f6 check, winning the king's cover by force.
Knight to the edge on b5 — a mistake. Play d4 instead, because on the rim the knight does nothing and gets kicked. Lesson: keep knights near the center.
Black puts a bishop on c5, aiming at your king side. Watch that bishop and meet it with your own pieces.
Ng3 is a big blunder — it lets Black win your bishop with check. Bd1 saves the bishop instead. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, move it to safety before anything else.
Ne2 is a fatal slip — it allows a forced mate. Qe2 was needed to block and trade. Lesson: when the enemy queen is near your bare king, count the mate threats first.

Castling queenside is a big mistake here. Black can play Bg4 to pin your queen, then win your rook with Bxd1; Nge2 was much safer. Lesson: don't castle into a spot where one move attacks your queen and rook.
Taking the knight with Bxd5 gives away your good bishop; Qf3 was better, keeping the bishop. Lesson: don't trade a strong bishop unless you must.
Black castles instead of grabbing your a2 pawn — a slow choice that helps you. Play Nc3 to bring your knight out and chase the black queen.
Grabbing the c7 pawn with Qxc7 looks tempting but is a mistake; Nc3 was better. Lesson: don't go pawn-hunting with your queen when your own pieces still need to get active.
Taking the b7 pawn with Qxb7 keeps the queen wandering and is again worse than Nc3. Lesson: one more pawn is not worth leaving your other pieces asleep.
This is the costly move of the game. f6 blocks your own pieces and opens lines near your king; far better was Be6 to develop the bishop and keep your big center solid.
A blunder — Nd2 blocks his own bishop and wastes time when c4 was needed. Seize the moment with Nd7, improving your knight toward the strong c5 square.

This is a big mistake. f4 drops material because after Nc4 your queen and bishop get forked and you lose the bishop on e3. Better was b3 to block the knight first. Lesson: before pushing pawns, check if it opens your own pieces to attack.
You developed your knight, but c5 was stronger to hit White's center right away. The center is getting big and needs to be challenged. Lesson: break a big center with a pawn before it gets strong.
Castling keeps your king safe, which is good, but the active Bg4 was even better. When you are doing well, keep up the pressure. Lesson: stay active even after castling.
White's knight attacks your queen but goes to the edge. Play Qb5 to keep your queen active and safe.

This knight jump looks scary but it loses a lot of value; Be4, keeping everything solid, was much better. You got lucky that White did not punish it. Lesson: before a fancy jump, check that your piece won't get into trouble.
White grabbed a pawn but left his rook in the corner. Take it: Nxa1 wins the whole rook.
Better was Nxb3 to free your trapped corner knight. As played, the knight stays stuck in the corner. Lesson: a trapped piece is worth saving, even by giving a little material back.
White wastes a move. Play b6 to break up his c5 pawn and open lines.
You try to run the corner knight out, but it just gets captured; b6 was much better. The c2 square was guarded. Lesson: check if a square is protected before you move there.
White pushes a pawn and overextends. Centralize with Qc4 to grab the initiative.
White pushes f5 and weakens himself. Hit back with Qc4 to attack.
Both rooks went passive; Qc4 was far more active. When you can attack, don't curl up. Lesson: in a good spot, keep making threats instead of retreating.
Big mistake by White. Take the pawn with exf5 and you are right back in the game.
Taking with the pawn (exf5) was safer and kept your structure; the rook capture lets White's queen jump to d6. Lesson: a pawn is often the safest piece to capture with.
Walking your king into the open is risky; Ref7, joining your rooks, was safer. Now your king is exposed. Lesson: in danger, bring defenders together, don't expose your king.
You save your rook — this is the best move in a tough spot.
Walking the king up runs into trouble and loses your rook; Qxf1+ to trade was the way to fight on. Lesson: when checked in danger, trading pieces is often the safest choice.
This knight jump is a mistake (better was Nbd7, bringing a piece out to help). Why: the knight on e4 gets kicked and you lose time.
They take your bishop, but this is a slip on their part. Just take back with the h-pawn (hxg6) and you are doing well.
They drop their bishop's guard — a mistake. Punish it with g5! The pawn attacks the bishop and wins you material.
You missed the strong g5 here. Why g5 was better: it hits their bishop and wins time, while this quiet knight move lets them off the hook.
Big mistake by them — they offer a queen trade on a bad square. Take it with check: Qxe3+ wins material!
This is a mistake — you should have taken the knight with Nxe4. Why: now their knight jumps to g5 and attacks your weak e6 pawn.
They jump the knight to fork your rooks, but it's a mistake! Grab the pawn first with Bxf2 — you come out ahead.
You missed the in-between Bxf2. Why: taking that pawn with the bishop first wins material before dealing with the fork.
A slow rook move by them. A good square for your knight now is d6.
Their king attacks your knight. The strong reply is the e5 pawn push.
You park the knight on d2, but Nh4 was better — it stays active and grabs a pawn.
They keep pushing their passer. Watch the race carefully.
They move the bishop poorly — a mistake. Just keep grabbing pawns with Kxg4.
You take the g-pawn. Good, you keep collecting material.
They race their pawn forward. You should rush your own pawn with g5.
You push your pawn ahead. It's your best try, but the position is hard now.
They give a check instead of the strongest move. Just step your king to safety with Kg3.
Your king goes to e3, but Kg3 was safer. Why: this exposes your king to more checks.
This is the game-losing move — your king walks into trouble and your pawn falls. Kf4 was needed. Lesson: in a race, keep your king close to your pawn and away from checks.
You move the king to h2, but Kf3 kept you more active. A small inaccuracy.
They check your king again. Stay calm and push your pawn.
You play Kg1, but Kg3 was better. Why: hiding in the corner gives them more checks.
Huge mistake by them — this check lets you queen! Play Kf2 and your pawn promotes next move.
You missed your golden chance — Kf2 would have made a new queen. This was the move to win or draw the game.
You step to g1 again, but Kg3 was a bit safer.
They reposition the bishop. The pressure stays on.
You retreat to g1, but Kg3 was better. Careful — a mate threat is coming.
The knight on the rim is in danger here. Ng8 was safer; on h5 his pawn g4 can trap it. Lesson: a knight on the edge has very few escape squares.
Lucky break — he missed g4, which would have won your knight! Now play g6 to give your knight a safe home.
Big gift! His e5 pawn is now hanging with check. Grab it: Qxe5+ wins a free pawn.
This pawn push weakens your king before it is safe. Castling first (O-O) was much better. Lesson: get your king to safety before opening lines near it.
This drops a pawn to a bishop check. Bf8 first was safer; now Bb5+ hits you. Lesson: before pushing a pawn, check for enemy checks it opens up.
He gives the check but it does not really hurt you. Block or step aside — play Kf7.
His bishop pins toward your knight, but this lets his edge slip. Defend with Bf6.
This loses a lot — the knight move lets his pawn fork your queen with f4. Bf6 was the solid defense. Lesson: keep your queen on safe squares where a pawn cannot hit it.
He gives back the advantage instead of trapping your queen. Slide your queen to safety with Qc7.
This pawn move lets his knight jump to b6 and fork your rook. Bd7 was safe. Lesson: watch for knight jumps that hit two pieces at once.
This ignores the threat and lets him win your rook. Rb8 had to save it. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, deal with it before doing anything else.
He pushes the pawn on the edge. Stay solid and keep an eye on his knight in the corner.
This drops a pawn to axb5. Bd7 was safer; now lines open near you. Lesson: count your defenders before pushing pawns on the side.
He grabs your pawn but loses some ground. Take back with your bishop.
This rook move drops a lot — Qb7 to trade queens was much better and calmer. Lesson: when behind or under pressure, trading queens makes defense easier.
He misses the strongest path. Now play Qb7 to offer the queen trade.
This lets him win your bishop with Rxa6. Qb7 was the saving move. Lesson: keep an eye on which of your pieces the enemy rook is aimed at.
You recapture, but Qc7 kept more material. Still, taking back is natural.
e5 is a real mistake. It does NOT defend the pawn — it pushes it where the knight can just grab it. Nc3 was right, guarding e4. Lesson: before pushing a pawn, check if it's actually protected.

Nc3 lets you lose more. Black's knight on e5 hits your bishop on c4, and your bishop wasn't safe. Be2 first would have saved material. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, move it or defend it before anything else.
Black plays Nc4 to save the knight — but this is a slip for Black. You can play Qb5! hitting the knight and getting active, winning back ground.
Nb5 is a mistake — it misses the strong Qb5 idea that pressured Black. Lesson: look for queen moves that attack two things at once before jumping a knight in.
Nc7 jumps in but it's loose — it doesn't really threaten enough. Qb3 was stronger, keeping pressure. Lesson: a knight deep in enemy land needs a real target, not just a 'looks scary' square.
Black plays Rb8 to defend, but this lets you back in — Qb3 keeps your attack alive and eyes weak points.
Nxe6 sacrifices the knight for a pawn — it's too hopeful here. Qc1 kept things together. Lesson: only give up a piece if you clearly see what you get back.
Black plays Ne4, a strong jump toward your king. Be careful: meet threats calmly, Qb4 keeps your queen active.
Qd1 is too passive and lets Black attack. O-O (castle) was urgent to hide your king. Lesson: when your king is in the open, getting it safe comes first.
Black plays Qb5, but it's not the best try. You can play Kg1 to tuck your king away and breathe.

Qe3 is a serious blunder — it puts the queen where Black's knight takes it with check: Nxe3+ wins your queen. f3 was needed. Lesson: before a queen move, check every enemy knight jump that gives check.
Be2 is a slow bishop move. This was your chance — push d5 to hit the center hard.
Qxf6 looks natural, but gxf6 was better — it keeps your pawns strong and your queen active. Lesson: when both recaptures are possible, think which keeps your pieces working best.
Bb5 pins your knight and looks scary, but it lets your queen jump to h6 with strong play. Qh6 was your best reply.
O-O puts your opponent's king in the corner — but it walked into your plan. The f4 jump is now very strong, so go Nf4.
Nxf2 sacrifices your knight, but it does not work here — you just lose material. Nf4 kept all your good pieces. Lesson: only sacrifice when you can clearly see it wins.
Bxf2+ wins one pawn back but trades off your strong bishop. h5 was steadier. After this you are still behind.
Rd3 is loose and lets a pawn fall. g5, gaining space, kept things tougher. Try to keep your pieces safe when behind.
Qc5+ gives a check but lets the queen be pushed back. Just step away with Kb8 and you're fine.
Rc8 pins the bishop but misses that your e5 pawn falls with check. Rxf3 first, grabbing the knight, was much better. Lesson: before you pin, check what your opponent can take.
Rd1 is a big slip by your opponent — it leaves the f7 bishop loose. Grab it: Rxf7 wins the piece!
Nd7+ gives a check but the knight can be met simply. Step the king to c7 and you're fine.
Rf1 keeps rooks on. This actually helps you — get your rook active with Rd2 on the second rank.
Rxa2 grabs a pawn but lets their rook check and grab your b7 pawn. b6 first, keeping things solid, was safer. Count what your opponent gets back before you grab.
Rf3 is a slip that wastes time. Bring your rook back with Re7 to stay coordinated.
Rd3 keeps the rook active for your opponent. Keep your two rooks working together and target their pawns.
Rc2 is a little loose; Ra3 tying down their pieces was better. Try to keep both rooks active and connected.
Kd6 walks the king into the open and lets the knight come with tempo. Kd8 was safer. Lesson: in the endgame the king is strong, but keep it away from checks and forks.
Rxh7 grabs another pawn, but it let your rook get active. Use Rg4 to attack and hold the passed pawns back.
g3 is slow and lets you get organized. Bring your other rook down with Rb2 for a strong setup.
h5 pushes the passed pawn, but it lets you crash in. Trade rooks with Rxd2+ and your own pawn races home.
Rxd2 recaptures, but this is losing for your opponent — your rook and b-pawn are too fast. Take the rook: Rxd2+ and push the pawn.
g4 pushes their pawns up the board. It's a race now — push your b-pawn and don't waste moves.
Kc7 loses precious time in a race. Pushing b4 right away was needed; their pawns got dangerous. Lesson: in a pawn race, every single move counts — push, don't shuffle.
g6 races their pawn forward and now it's very close. You must push your b-pawn fast and watch for their queen.
Rg8 tries to stop the pawn, but your king belonged in front (Kd6). The race got scary. Use your rook and king together to stop their runners.
Kh4 marches their king up to help the pawns. Keep pushing b and keep your rook ready to block.
Kg5 brings their king closer to shepherd their pawns. Push on with b3.
h6 pushes their second runner. Both sides are close; push b2 and get ready to queen.
Rxg6+ is a big blunder — it throws away your rook and the win. Re8, stopping the h-pawn, kept you winning. Lesson: don't give up a rook unless it clearly wins on the spot.
The queen on d3 sits in an awkward spot and drops some advantage. Better was Ne2: it keeps your pieces tidy and avoids letting them mess up your pawns.
They put the queen on e7, which is passive and loses ground. You can punish this by pushing e5 to grab space and attack.
Big mistake! They grabbed your e4 pawn with the bishop, but it loses material. Win it with Rxe4 — after Nxe4 Qxe4 you come out ahead.
They miss their chance and play Nc6 instead. Now you can grab a free pawn with Qxb5.
Qg3 misses it. You should have taken the pawn with Qxb5 — it was just hanging there for free.
Re1 is slow here. The strong move was Ne5, planting your knight in a powerful central spot.
Blunder by them with Na5. Punish it right away with Bxd5, winning the pawn and getting a great bishop.
Big blunder! Bd6 puts your bishop where it can simply be taken. Better was Be4, keeping the bishop safe and strong. Lesson: before moving, check if the square is defended.
Ne5 is okay but Be4 was better, putting the bishop on a strong central line.
Nxf7 gives the knight away for nothing — they just take with Rxd5. The calm Bf3 was much better. Lesson: don't sacrifice unless you see a clear payoff.
Qe5 leaves your knight hanging — they win it with Rxg4. Better was Ne5 to keep the knight safe and active.
Big mistake by Black! His queen comes out but leaves his pieces loose. Punish it with Qd4 — your queen guards your knight and stays in control with extra material.
You move the queen, but Qd4 was much better — it would have kept your knight safe and held your edge. Lesson: when ahead, protect the piece that is hanging first.
Another slip by Black — he takes with the pawn and forgets his knight on e4. It is now undefended: grab it with check by Qxe4+!
You step the queen back. The active Qf4 was a bit better, but you are still clearly ahead.

This loses material. Pushing b4 opens the long dark diagonal straight to your rook in the corner. After Bxb4 cxb4 Black plays Qxa1 and wins your rook. Nd2 was safe. Lesson: before a pawn move, check what diagonals or lines it opens toward your own pieces.
Black drifts with the queen to the side; this was a little loose for him. Keep playing solid moves.

This is too passive and lets Black push d4 to attack your knight. Re2 was much better, kicking the queen and staying active. Lesson: don't hide a piece in the corner when you can challenge the enemy queen instead.
This drops the knight. After Qc4 Black just plays dxc3 and wins it. Qe4 first was the saving move. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, defend or move it before making other plans.
Black brings the queen over; this wandered a bit, Rd8 was better for him. Stay solid.
A loose pawn move that weakens your king a little. Bd4, centralizing the bishop, was stronger. Lesson: avoid pawn moves near your king unless you must.
Black pushes a pawn, but this loses it — take it with bxa5! Free pawn for you.
You dodge the trade, but Qxb5 was the move — trading queens makes the game much easier. Lesson: when the position is even or you want calm, trading queens removes the danger.
This misses the free a-pawn — bxa5 was clearly better and just wins it. Lesson: don't forget about easy pawns you can grab while you maneuver.
Bd7 was a costly move; after axb5 your pawns crumble. Much better was b4, keeping the chain and gaining space. Lesson: when a pawn is attacked, push or defend it, don't ignore it.
White castled but missed axb5, which would have won material. You should grab the chance now: bxa4 wins back a pawn and frees you.
White plays c4 but again skips the winning axb5. Take with bxc4 right away to grab the pawn and ease your cramped position.
Big gift! White plays Qxd6 — but his queen can simply be taken. Grab it at once with cxd6.
Knight to g4 runs to a bad square where it gets chased. Better was Nd5, a calm strong home in the middle. Lesson: when chased, pick a safe square, not a far one.
White plays h3 to kick your knight, but this leaves the e5 pawn loose. Punish it now with Ngxe5 and just win the pawn.
White takes with the queen — but the queen comes out too early. Punish it with Nc6, which retreats your attacked knight AND hits the queen, winning time.
You push e5, which weakens your own squares and lets White's knight target them. d5 was stronger and safer. Lesson: don't push pawns that leave holes behind.
White's knight heads toward your king side. Stay alert — it wants to jump to g5.
Rook to e8 looks tidy but takes your eye off your king. Qe6 was better to guard the king side. Lesson: when an attack is near, defend first.
White's knight leaps to g5 and now eyes a deadly Qxh7. You MUST play h6 right now to kick the knight away.
This is the losing move. You missed the threat — h6 was needed to chase the knight and stop the attack. Now White mates. Lesson: before your own move, always ask 'what does my opponent threaten?'
Knight to g5 was a mistake — it attacks nothing real and wastes time. Simply castling (O-O) was much better and safer. Lesson: don't push a knight forward unless it makes a real threat.
You castled, which is good, but the moment for a kingside pawn push (h4) was even stronger. Still, a safe king is never wrong.
Black's rook comes to c8, eyeing the open c-file toward your king side. Watch that file — your c2 pawn and back rank need care.
Taking the pawn with Nxg5 was a real mistake — you give up a knight for not enough. Just play h4 to meet the pawn. Lesson: don't sacrifice a piece unless you clearly see what you get back.
Queen to e3 was a slip that drops your edge; the pawn push h4 to fight for the h-file was much better. Lesson: when an open file points at your king, fight for it fast.
Black retreats the knight to e7, planning to reroute it. You have a moment — grab it by playing f4 to open lines and stay active.

The pawn push g4 was a serious mistake — it weakens your king and lets Black's knights swarm in. The knight to a5 (hitting the b7 bishop) was far better. Lesson: don't push pawns in front of your own king when enemy pieces are near.
Black grabs your c2 pawn with the rook — a greedy move that you can punish. Trade off the strong f4 knight first with Bxf4 to ease the attack.
Queen to e3 was a costly mistake — it lets Black check and win material with Qxg4+. Playing h3 to cover g4 was needed. Lesson: always check what checks your opponent has before moving.

Rook to f1 was a blunder that loses the game — it walks into a winning attack. The knight to a1, regrouping, was needed. Lesson: when defending, check that your move doesn't open new lines to your king.
You play the small d3 instead of d4. Pushing d4 was much stronger because it claims the center; d3 is too timid. Lesson: when you can take the center, take it.
You play g3, weakening the squares around your king. Better was Nf3 to fix the knight first. Lesson: don't loosen pawns near your king without a clear reason.
You grab the a6 pawn with the bishop, but this gives up your good bishop for little. Taking on c6 first was cleaner. Lesson: think before trading your best piece for a pawn.
Black plays Nd4, but this loses material. Punish it: take the knight with Bxd4, and you can also grab the c7 pawn soon.
You castle long instead of grabbing c7. Safe-looking, but Qxc7 was stronger and just wins a pawn. Lesson: when a free pawn is on offer with no danger, take it.
Black blunders with Kf8 instead of Kd8. You can play Qd7 and then snap up the c7 pawn with a great position.
You take the c7 pawn with the queen, but this lets Black hit back; f4 first was stronger. Be careful grabbing pawns when your own king side is loose.
Black tucks the king to g8. This drops the thread; you can reset with Qd7 and stay on top.
Black moves the king to h7. This wanders the king into danger; open the position with f4.
You play Re2, but it allows a trade that helps Black. The pawn push f4 was much stronger. Lesson: keep the initiative with pawn breaks, not slow rook moves.
Black blunders by taking the h2 pawn. Punish with Qf5+, giving check and keeping your attack rolling.
Black blunders badly with Qh5, walking into trouble. Punish with Re7 — your rook storms in on the 7th and your attack is huge.
You push g4, missing the strong Re7. The rook on the 7th rank was crushing; g4 lets Black escape. Lesson: look for active rook moves before pushing pawns.
You play Re6 instead of trading. The queen trade Qxf7+ was clearly better and simpler. Lesson: when ahead, trading queens makes winning easier.
You play Rg6, but f6 was stronger to support your passed pawn. Try to push your far pawns with the rook behind them.
You push f6 instead of taking the g5 pawn. Rxg5 was better to kill Black's dangerous pawn. Lesson: stop the enemy passed pawn before it runs.
Black blunders with Kf7. Punish by taking the bishop with fxg7 — you win the piece.
You take the bishop with Rxg7+ check. It wins material, but fxg7 was even cleaner. Still, you are winning.
Black grabs the d5 pawn with the king. This wastes time; swing your rook behind the h-pawn with Re1.
You play Re1 to get behind the passed pawn — correct, this stops it.
Black pushes g4, but this lets you make progress. Push your c-pawn — c3 is the way to break through.
You play b4. Pushing c3 was stronger to open lines faster, but b4 still keeps the win.
Black's king reaches e5. No matter; push your pawns to promote.
You push c4. A small inaccuracy — b7 right away was faster to promote, but you are still winning.
c3 is a real blunder. It does nothing while your pawn can charge forward. Push e4 to fork his bishop and knight at once.
Ng5 is another blunder. It does not save both pieces. Just take with exd3 and win a piece.
d4 pushes a pawn, but he missed Kxh1 to win your knight. You still have a chance — play Nf2 to free it.
Qc8 is a big mistake. It lets him win your bishop on d7. Be6 would have saved the piece. Lesson: when a piece is attacked, guard it or move it.
Qa6 wanders off and loses more ground. Rd8 to fight his rook was much better.
Qb3 is a blunder back. Now you can grab with cxd4 and open lines on his king.
c4 hits the queen but cxd4 was stronger. Still okay.
Nc6 is a blunder — it forks nothing useful and lets you check. Play Rb1+ to attack his king.
Bg5 is a big slip — it lets his knight grab your a7 pawn for free. Bh4+ keeping the check going was far stronger.
Nxa7 takes your pawn, but it walks the knight away into the corner — a blunder. Bring your rook in with Rb2 to attack.
g3 weakens his king but he should have saved the knight. Get your rook active with Rb2.
Rxe3 grabs a pawn but lets his rook check and trade off. Rb2 was stronger. This let the game slip.
Qxd2 grabs a piece but misses Qe6+, which was far better. This let his rook escape with a check of its own.
Qd7+ is a costly check — it lets his king escape your net. Bd8 was the strong move to keep squeezing.
Kd7 is a blunder — it loses his d4 pawn. Take it with Qxd4+.
g5 pushes a pawn, but h5 was the right pawn to run. Small slip in the race.
Ne7+ is a blunder — the knight is undefended. Take it with Bxe7.
Bxd5 is the big mistake of the game. The pawn was guarded by their queen, so after Qxd5 you simply lose your bishop for nothing. Lesson: before you capture, check what is defending the piece.
They blunder with Ne4 — a big slip. You can grab the center and chase the knight with d4, gaining time and space.
They play Bc5, slightly loose. You can hit the center with d4 and start to take over.
They blunder with Kd8, walking their king into danger. You can play d3 to free your bishop and start an attack.
Ne5 is tempting but d3 was much better to open your pieces. The knight jump lets them off the hook a little. Lesson: develop your sleeping pieces before chasing.
They blunder badly with Re8 — this drops material. Jump in with Nxf7+, a fork that checks the king and grabs the rook!
They blunder with Kc7, leaving the king exposed. Check with Bf4+ to harass the king and gain time.
Ng5 looks aggressive but Bf4+ was the strong check. The knight wanders to the edge and loses some punch. Lesson: a check that gains time often beats a fancy jump.
They play h6 to kick your knight, another inaccuracy. You can still play Bf4+ to check and keep pressing.
Nf3 retreats the knight safely, but Bf4+ was the better, more active choice. Try not to let attacking chances cool off.
They blunder huge with Bxh2 — the bishop has no escape after you take. Grab it with Nxh2 and win a whole piece!
They blunder with Rg8, leaving the g4 bishop loose again. Centralize with Bd4 to pile up and then take on e5.
They blunder with Re8 — now the bishop falls. Take it with Nxg4 and win the piece!
White's queen wanders to a bad square and badly misjudges it. Punish at once with Be7, attacking the queen and gaining time.
White's queen runs away again and drops more. Now play f5 to set up winning his weak d3 pawn.
White gives a check but simply loses the bishop. Just take it with Nxc6.
White grabs a pawn but it is risky and loses ground. Win the c6 pawn back with Qxc6.
This bishop move is too slow — Kf7 was much better. Your king in the center is the real danger, not the bishop. Lesson: solve king safety before anything else.
White makes a small pawn move and badly drops his edge. Take the chance with Kf7 to get your king safe and solid.
White moves the knight and blunders badly. Punish with the check Qc5+, then you win the queen on a7.
You captured White's queen — a huge material win! Even better was Qc5+ first (check, then take), but you are now clearly winning. Lesson: when a check comes with the capture, play the check first.
White moves his rook and blunders. Punish with Bd4, attacking the rook — you win it with Bxe3+ next.

White plays Be3, which is a real mistake — it blocks nothing useful and drops the lead. The bishop on e3 can be hit. The strong reply is Bc5, pinning that bishop and piling on. Lesson: when the opponent misplaces a piece, attack it fast.
You play Ng4, attacking the e3 bishop. It is okay, but Bc5 was much better — it pinned the bishop and gave you a bigger edge. Still, your knight makes a threat.
You play Bd7, a quiet developing move, but it misses the free pawn. Qxe3 was much better — it wins a pawn and keeps your queen strong. Lesson: look for the capture first before making a calm move.
White castles, O-O, getting the king safe. But White still left that e3 pawn hanging. You can take it with check next.
You play Qb6, but this lets White's rook grab your f7 pawn with Rxf7. Better was to castle long, O-O-O, getting your king safe first. Lesson: get your king tucked away before the position opens up.
White plays b4 instead of taking on f7 — a let-off for you. Castle long now with O-O-O to finally make your king safe. Lesson: when given a second chance, take it.

You play Bb5, but this lets White take your b7 pawn with check, Bxb7+. Better was Qh6, keeping your queen active and safe. Lesson: check what the opponent's bishop is aiming at before moving elsewhere.
White plays Bxb7+, winning your b7 pawn with check. You must take the bishop back with your queen, Qxb7, and life goes on. Lesson: always answer a check first.

White grabs your f7 pawn with Rxf7, a greedy move that lets you fight back. The engine likes Qd5, centralizing your queen to attack and defend at once. Lesson: when a rook goes pawn-hunting, look for an active queen move.
You play Bd6, eyeing White's king, but Qd5 was stronger to hit more targets at once. Your bishop does point at a nice diagonal though.
White plays Rxf8, trading rooks. This actually helps you a bit — just recapture. Take back with Rxf8 and keep your pieces working.
You play Rb4, going after the pawns, but it lets White push a5. A check with Rh5+ first was better to gain time. Your rook does target the pawns though.
You play Ka8, but this walks into the corner trap. Kb8 was safer and kept you fighting. Lesson: in the corner the king has no air, so avoid it when pawns are pushing.
White plays Kc6, bringing the king up to help mate, but it eases the pressure for a moment. Try to free your bishop and king; Bd8 gives a little defense.

You play Rxb7, but this is the losing move — after axb7+ and Kb8, White plays Ra8 mate. The safe move was Ka7. Lesson: before taking a pawn, ask 'what does my opponent do next?' Taking opened the mate.
Big blunder! With g6 they let your knight fork both rooks. Play Nf7 to win the exchange (rook for knight).
Your biggest mistake. Better was Rc3+ with a check. Pushing g4 lets their rook and pawns get active. Lesson: keep the initiative with checks when you can.
Blunder! Now you can win the bishop: play Rxd6+. After cxd6, Rxd6+ wins it all back with profit.
Their bishop checks again from e7. Just move your king; their position is lost anyway.
Blunder again with Bd6+! This time grab it: Rxd6+, then after cxd6 you play Rxd6+ and win the piece.
Black pushes e5 right next to your pawn — a mistake that just gives a pawn away. Take it: dxe5 wins a free pawn.
Bringing the queen to d2 is slow. Nb5 was stronger — it jumps in to attack the d6 bishop. Lesson: look for active knight jumps before quiet queen moves.
You castle your king to safety — a good idea, though the pin Bg5 was a bit sharper. Still, king safety is never wrong.
Black's h6 is a wasted little pawn move. Now Nd4 is strong — your knight jumps to the center, eyeing c6 and e6.
Nb5 is not as good. Nd4, putting the knight in the strong center, was much better. Lesson: a knight in the center is worth more than one on the edge.
Black's Bf5 lets you trade rooks with Rxd8+ and then get active — take that chance.
Black's Bg4 does not really threaten anything. Qc4 is a strong, active square for your queen.
Big mistake. a3 leaves your e3 pawn open to Qxe3+, winning it with check. The move e4 was needed to guard the center. Lesson: before a quiet pawn move, check that nothing hangs.
Lucky for you! Black missed Qxe3+, which wins a pawn with check. Now play e4 to fix your center.
Bd3 develops, but your e3 pawn still hangs to Qxe3+. Play e4 right now to save it.
Black again skips Qxe3+ and trades knights instead. Just take back with exd4.
Black missed the Qe3+ check one more time. You are safe now.
Qa4 is okay, but Qc5 — offering a queen trade into a good ending — was cleaner.
Black's king walks to a7. Use the moment to bring your rook into play with Re1.
Nb5+ just checks and gets chased back. Qa5, improving the queen, was better than this repeat.
Black's king wanders to a7 again.
Be4 offers a trade. Rd1, grabbing the open file, was stronger — your rook was sitting idle.
Black puts the bishop back on e6.
Black's rook on d5 is loose. Hit it with Nc3 — the rook must run, and you can win it for your knight.
Nc5 misses it. c4 attacks the loose rook on d5 and wins material. Lesson: when you spot a loose enemy piece, chase it at once.
Black plays b6 to attack your knight, but this lets you grab the bishop with dxe6 — take it.
You take on e6 with the knight, but dxe6 was better — taking with the pawn kept your strong knight.
Black's Re2 lets you trade rooks with Rxe2; after Qxe2 you then play Qxc7+, winning a pawn with check. Grab it.
Rd1 misses it. Rxe2 first — trade rooks, then Qxc7+ wins a pawn with check. Lesson: look for trades that end in a winning check.
A huge gift! Black's Qe2 lets you checkmate: Qxc7+ Ka8 then Rd8#. Play Qxc7+ — it is mate in two!
Big mistake. The bishop pin does not help, and now White can win back the f4 pawn. Better was g5 to defend that pawn. Lesson: protect your extra pawn before pinning.
You step the bishop back instead. This drops your edge. Taking with Bxf3 first was much stronger.
White blunders with e5. Just take it: dxe5 wins a pawn cleanly.
White blunders with Bb5. Answer with Bb4 to pin and stay on top.
White blunders again with e6. Just take it: fxe6 and you are clearly better.
Mistake. This check lets the king run free. Bf8 kept the king trapped and was much stronger. Lesson: in the endgame, trap the king, don't chase it.
White blunders into a mating net. There is a forced mate: Bf3+ then Bg5 is checkmate! Find it.
Mistake. This loses your rook, because the king just takes it on g5. Rxe5 saved the rook. Lesson: always check if your piece is hanging.
White blunders with Rf7+. Just take it: Bxf7+ wins the rook with check!
White makes a quiet, slow pawn move. You can grab the lead in development — Bb4 comes out with a pin.

Mistake: you gave up your strong bishop for the knight. Bd6 was better, keeping the bishop, because now your e5 pawn becomes weak. Lesson: bishops are valuable — don't trade them for knights without a reason.
White wastes a move — he could have grabbed your e5 pawn with Nxe5. Use the free time: play Nc6 to develop and defend e5.
Slow move. The knight to d5 was much stronger — it hits the bishop and lands on a great square. Lesson: that Nd5 jump has been your best plan for many moves.

Big mistake! This lets White trap your queen with Bg2 (then Qxg2 Rxg2 and your queen is lost). h5 was safe and best. Lesson: before moving other pieces, always check if your queen can be attacked and trapped.
Lucky for you — White missed Bg2, which would have won your queen! Save it now with the check Qf6+.
You activate the rook, but your queen was still in danger; the check Qf6+ to get it safe was urgent.
You grab a pawn, but Be4 was stronger; this lets White trade and ease his game.
A check that keeps you active; Qg2+ was a little better, but this is fine.
Huge blunder by White! He offers a queen trade that you win — take it with Qxd2+ and you'll be up a whole queen.
White's king shuffles; the mate is getting close.
You grab another pawn; still totally winning, though a check was quicker.
White just pushes a pawn; nothing changes, you are winning.
You push your passed pawn to make a second-queen threat. Fine.
White's king steps into danger; keep driving it toward the edge.
Checkmate! You won the game. Lesson: you used your extra queen and pawn to trap the king on the edge — well done finishing it off.
Careful! Knight to b5 walks into trouble and loses a lot. The simple b4 was much stronger — it keeps your queenside attack rolling and stays safe.
They play a6 to hit your knight, but this is a mistake. Push a5 to trap and win their bishop on b6 (a5 Ba7 then your knight takes it).
Rook to e1 is too slow and lets things slip. The crushing a5 was there — it forks the bishop and pins the b6 spot, winning material.
Huge blunder — they grab a pawn and ignore the danger. Now you have checkmate: knight takes e7!
Black develops the knight but leaves the e5 pawn loose. Here you could play d4! After d4 and Nxe5 you win that pawn for free.
Re1 is slow and misses the win. The strong move was d4 — then Nxe5 grabs a free pawn, just like the move before.
Bxd5 gives away your good Italian bishop. Better was Nd2 to keep the bishop and stay solid.
g3 lets the attack come. The strong move was Qf3 — it grabbed the lead and hit Black's loose bishop.
